session_note: The 153rd Delaware General Assembly (2025-2026) is a two-year carryover body: bills introduced in the 2025 session remain alive through the 2026 session without refiling. Del. Const. art. II, section 4 requires the General Assembly to adjourn sine die no later than 5:00 p.m. on the last day of June each year; for 2026 that deadline (June 30) was met via Delaware's customary stopped-clock practice, with the final legislative day's floor votes recorded on legis.delaware.gov as occurring into the small hours of July 1, 2026. Any bill not enacted by that sine die adjournment dies with the biennium and must be reintroduced from scratch in the 154th General Assembly (2027) -- Delaware does not carry individual bills into a third year.

decisions.notes: SB 205 (Public Service Commission certificate-to-operate requirement for large energy users, as amended by Senate Amendment 1 to a 100 MW / transmission-certificate threshold) never received a floor vote after being placed on the Ready List on 2026-03-11. Unlike the group of large-energy-user/data-center bills (including the HB 233 substitute and SB 312) that were pushed through on the 153rd General Assembly's final 2026 legislative day, SB 205 is absent from the official bill page's action history beyond the Ready List entry, and no news coverage of the final-day votes lists it among the bills passed. Per Delaware's sine die rule, it is therefore dead for the biennium and would need to be reintroduced in the 154th General Assembly (2027). Confidence is 0.75 rather than higher because the official page displays only a summary history rather than an exhaustive session journal, so a very-last-minute action cannot be ruled out with certainty; no corroborating news of passage was found.

new_bills.key_provisions: Amends Title 9, Title 22, and Title 29 of the Delaware Code relating to data centers. Prohibits state agencies, counties, and municipalities from entering into nondisclosure agreements that would restrict public access to information about potential or actual large-scale data center development (defined by reference to facilities capable of using 100+ MW), aiming to preserve local transparency and public input into data-center siting decisions.
